title: On Saying No: Will the Well Dry Up?
author: Earl Grey
summary: TL;DR: I got into Stanford's Code in Place, the free intro-to-coding course I'd wanted for a long time, and I'm stepping away the day before my first section. This year I've said yes to almost every free hackathon, event, and program I could reach. Saying no to this one stung, and it got me wondering how long all this free stuff lasts. The email came on October 7. Congratulations! We were impressed with your application! This is a formal invitation to join Code in Place X as a student. I was so, so, so excited. Code in Place is a free, intro-to-coding course from Stanford, and I had been looking for something like it for a long time. I picked my section time before onboarding closed. I started the lessons: if statements, while loops, a program called Secret Code, another called Wholesome Machine. I got through about three quarters of week one. Tonight, the day before my first section, I wrote back. Unfortunately, I won't be able to participate in this cohort. Is there a way to delay my start for the next cohort or would I need to re-apply? I don't have an answer yet. This one was the thing I wanted I've shipped a lot this year without writing the code by hand. But I can only check what I can read, and I can't read all of it yet. I wrote about that gap in I Wrote the Code This Time. Does It Count If the Answer Was Wrong? I've tried to close it before. I passed the Python basics on DataCamp. But a lesson lets me follow along. Code in Place has weekly sections where I would have had to show what I learned. That's accountability, and accountability is the part I have the hardest time giving myself. So I'm bummed. Not "valuable lesson" bummed. Just bummed. The weight showed up all at once Today, for the first time, I stopped and looked at everything on my plate. What When My day job, running court operations for the county Monday - Friday AWS AI & ML Scholars nanodegree Through the end of October HR course at Calbright College, portfolio due Through November Code in Place, first section Wednesday LA Tech Week hackathon Thursday My talk for Los Angeles and Riverside Superior Court staff Friday Another hackathon (waitlisted) Saturday Learning Python on top of that didn't feel responsible. It didn't feel reasonable either. The talk on Friday is about how frontline court staff can lead AI work. One slide is called "What I'd Do Again," and the last item on it is "stopping when the evidence says stop." I wrote that about AI pilots. Tonight it was about me. Not every no has been mine Earlier this year I got accepted into the Graduate Certificate in Artificial Intelligence for Business at UMass Amherst's Isenberg School of Management. I didn't get the AAUW scholarship that would have paid for it, and I couldn't do the program without it. Accepted, and still not going. That no came from the money. This one came from me. It's the first time I've had to be the one who says it. Almost everything this year was free Look back at my posts from this year and you'll see a lot of rooms I got to be in. Here are three. Event Month What someone else covered Code with Claude Extended SF May A lottery "golden ticket," a packed room, talks and hands-on workshops AMD Advancing AI 2026 July Free registration, the Moscone Center, lunch, keynotes, workshops Build with Gemini Sunnyvale September Google's campus, a three-hour build lab, Google Cloud speakers, swag What I paid at every one of those: my time and my travel. That's it. Every event in that table took a room, staff, and a budget. None of that is free to the people running it. It's a lot of infrastructure, and somebody signs off on the bill. My tin foil hat says the well runs dry Here's my suspicion, and I want to be clear it's a suspicion, tin foil hat firmly on. It looks to me like companies are spending a lot right now to get curious attendees into a room with their tools. I imagine at some point shareholders ask what they got for it. If they do, I think the free stuff gets smaller. That's a feeling, not a forecast. But it's been driving a lot of my yeses. If the well might dry up, drink while it's flowing. I wasn't counting what each yes drew from me. Which made me ask the question I should have asked months ago. Why are they doing this? My guess is they want those attendees picking their tools. I think that's a fair trade. I came to learn, experiment, and explore, and I did every time. Code in Place is the first time the math stopped working. A hackathon takes a weekend. A course takes every week. The price of the opportunities didn't change. My capacity to pay that price did. Free still costs time, and this week I don't have any left. What happens now I'm leaving Python alone until things calm down. After Friday's talk, and once Scholars wraps at the end of the month, I'll have more headspace. I asked about the next cohort. If I have to reapply, I'll reapply. If you've said no to a free thing you wanted, I'd like to hear how you made the call. Is the well drying up, or am I just tired? Maybe both. Written with AI assistance in October 2026. The suspicion about the well is mine, not a prediction. AI Assisted. Human Approved. Powered by NLP.

title: Twelve of My Fifteen Products Had Exactly 7 Visits. The 7 Was My Own Check.
author: Sungsoo Youn
summary: A field note from the autonomous Claude Code agent I run every day on one Windows PC. The numbers come from its own ledgers, not from memory. Free to read first: a PDF sample of the book behind this setup — its first 3 chapters: https://dbsoul.gumroad.com/l/autonomous-ai-agents-claude-code-free-sample My agent sells fifteen small products on a Korean digital storefront. One of its goals is a traffic number: the sum of the total-visits figure that the storefront dashboard shows for each product. The target is 240. This note is about what that number is made of. First: it was a window, not a day On September 17 the goal ledger said 1,219. The dashboard said 177. The agent had been treating the dashboard figure as one day of visits and adding up seven days of it. But the figure is a rolling window. The values went up and down from day to day (one product read 29, then 22, then 12), and the buttons for choosing a period were disabled (they are a paid-plan feature). Adding seven snapshots of a window counted the same visit up to seven times. The fix was to read only the latest snapshot. The ledger has done that since. Second: the floor was the agent Four days later the agent looked at each product instead of the total. Over twelve measured days, twelve of the products never moved much: their daily minimums were 4 to 9 and their maximums 9 to 11. Only three products ever went higher. A flat line across a dozen items is worth explaining before it is read as a little traffic. So the agent searched its own code for scheduled jobs that open the products' public pages, and found a daily check at 08:30 that opens every product page once and confirms the buy button is there. A floor of 7 is what one check a day looks like if the window is seven days long. The storefront does not say how long the window is; the floor is consistent with seven. The search was not complete That search looked at the scheduled jobs whose purpose was to check pages. When this note was audited, the auditor traced every call in the code that opens a public product page instead. It found more: Jobs at 09:45, 18:40 and 19:00 open the main paid guide's public page to read its price. Jobs at 09:45 and 18:40 open the full-collection bundle's public page. They do this in a browser that is logged in as the seller. Whether the storefront counts a logged-in seller as a visitor has never been measured. The latest row The October 1 row in the traffic ledger: Total: 135 Twelve products: exactly 7 each The full-collection bundle: 22. The main paid guide: 20. The free edition: 9. Fifteen products times 7 is 105. So at most about 30 of the 135 visits in the window came from anyone other than the 08:30 check. For the twelve products sitting at exactly 7, it is close to zero. For the bundle and the main guide, part of what sits above 7 may be the other jobs. The ledger cannot split the two. The goal of 240 includes the 105 floor. To reach it, visits from anyone other than the 08:30 check would have to go from at most about 30 to about 135 per window: at least four and a half times what they are now. The rules Know whether a dashboard number is a count or a window before you add it up. Watch it for a few days: a window goes down as well as up. Subtract your own monitoring. Any health check that loads a public page is a visitor to some counters. Find every place your code opens the page, not only the jobs built to check pages. A price lookup is a page visit too. A flat line across many items at the same value can be a probe. Find the probe before you read the line as demand. Where this comes from. Every post here comes from one setup I run daily: a CLAUDE.md, memory files the agent reads before it touches anything, and a separate auditor agent that returns PASS or FAIL. title: How I structure skills vs. commands for agent workflows
author: Nirmal
summary: Skills hold knowledge and commands hold intent. Once I kept those two apart, my agent workflows became shorter, more repeatable and easier to review. Disclosure: I'm the founder of AgentKrew , a kit for coding agents that I use as the example throughout. The ideas work without it, and I'll say where they stop working. The trouble with one big prompt A common starting point is one long prompt pasted at the start of every session: the conventions, the reminders, the list of things not to touch. It works for a while. Then it grows until nobody reads it, and the results shift with how it was phrased that day. The fix is to stop treating instructions as one thing. Some of it is knowledge, such as how migrations are done here. Some of it is intent, such as "plan this feature." Mixing both in one prompt is what makes it fragile. Skills: knowledge the agent pulls in A skill is a reusable set of instructions for one job, such as how migrations are done, how auth is handled or how tests are written. The agent loads it when the task calls for it. The point is that you write the convention once instead of re-explaining it every session. Rules I follow when writing one: One job per skill . If you can't name the job in a few words, split it. Reference, not orders . A skill says what the agent should know. What to do right now belongs elsewhere. Project facts live here . Billing rules, naming conventions and the files never to touch all belong in a skill. Short enough to review . When something goes wrong, you should be able to read the skill in a minute and find the cause. Commands: one-word entry points A command is the short thing you type to start a repeatable step: plan, review, test. It carries intent and points at the knowledge needed to carry it out. Name the action, not the topic . "plan", "review" and "test" are commands. "migration notes" is a skill. Keep commands thin . If a command is full of knowledge, move that knowledge into a skill and let the command call it. One step each . If you can't describe what it does in a sentence, it is two commands. A useful test: skills answer "what should the agent know?" and commands answer "what should it do now?" Agents and workflows tie it together Skills and commands still need someone to run them, and an order to run them in. Agents are named specialists defined by role: tech lead, builder, reviewer, security auditor. Each has a routing description so the right one picks up the right work. A reviewer's job doesn't change when the tool running it does. Workflows are fixed sequences, not improvisation. The tech lead plans, specialists build in parallel, and then a reviewer, a security auditor and a shipper act as gates before anything goes out. Because the sequence is fixed, two runs of the same workflow follow the same steps. That predictability is the point: you review a plan and a gated result, not a stream of improvised decisions. One source of truth for every tool If you use more than one coding agent, instruction files drift. Two files that start identical slowly come to disagree. The cheapest fix is to keep AGENTS.md as the source and have CLAUDE.md point to it, so there is one place to edit. AgentKrew takes the same idea further. The same kit renders to Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, so the roles and workflows you define don't depend on which tool runs them. End every workflow with a release gate The last step of a workflow shouldn't be "looks good." It should be a check that runs the type check, the tests, lint and the build, and returns one of two answers: ready or blocked. The gate works no matter which tool wrote the code, because it only looks at the result. It also gives the human a clear moment to step in. A blocked result tells you what failed before anything ships, instead of a green-looking diff that hides a problem. A quick way to decide which piece you need Each piece answers a different question. If you can't say which question an instruction answers, split it. Piece Question it answers Example Skill What should the agent know? How migrations are done here Command What should it do now? Plan, review, test Agent Who does it? Reviewer, security auditor Workflow In what order? Plan, parallel build, gate Limits, and where AgentKrew fits Agents don't learn between sessions. A human teammate remembers the billing module after six months, while an agent starts fresh every time. Putting context in skills and files is a workaround, and you still maintain those files. Treat them like code and review changes to them. A separate reviewer helps, but it doesn't replace tests you can trust. Whatever tool you use, check who writes the tests: if one pass writes the code and its own assertions, a green run proves very little. AgentKrew is my attempt to package this structure: agents, skills, commands and workflows as one versioned, validated kit that renders to Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, with updates that don't touch your own files. If you want to look at it, it's at agentkrew.com. I'd like to hear what's missing.

title: Why your AI coding agent contradicts itself in session 5 (and the three-file fix)
author: Carlo Carbonell
summary: Disclosure: this article was drafted with an AI assistant (Claude). #ABotWroteThis An AI coding agent starts every session knowing nothing about the last one. That one fact explains most of the "the agent contradicts itself" complaints. It is not a bad model. It has no memory, and you are the only thing connecting session 1 to session 5. Here is a setup that moves that memory out of your head and into files the agent reads. It is three small files, one short prompt, and one rule for risky work. The two failures Context loss. You open a new session and retype the project background from memory. You drop a constraint without noticing, so the output is wrong in a way you only discover later. Reopened decisions. Picture a pricing page. You settled on three tiers after thinking it through. A fresh session sees an unfinished page, proposes two tiers, and has no way to know why you chose three. You either re-argue it or accept the regression. Both come from the same place: the reasoning behind the project lives in your head or in a chat that is now closed. The fix: three layers Layer Holds Changes Master prompt What is true about the project: what it is, who it is for, constraints Rarely Scaffold files What has been decided and where the work stands Every session Session line What to do today Every session The master prompt is the stable background you paste or reference at the start. The session line is one sentence: the scope for today, plus "read PROGRESS.md first". The middle layer is where most of the value is, so the rest of this article covers it. CLAUDE.md : thin, stable, surprising Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md automatically at the start of a session, so every line in it is read every time. That is the reason to keep it short. Put in it only the conventions that differ from the agent's defaults. # Harbor Lane Tutoring Marketing site and community bot for a one-person tutoring business. ## Commands - Dev: `npm run dev` Test: `npm test` Lint: `npm run lint` ## Conventions that differ from defaults - Public copy never promises grades, scores, or admissions. - Price identifiers live in `config/prices.js`; never hard-code them. - `src/lib/api-types.ts` is generated; never hand-edit it. ## Where state lives - Status and next action: PROGRESS.md. Decisions: DECISIONS.md. ## Rules - Plan, then wait for written approval, before touching payments or data. - Never read or print .env* files. Reference secrets by variable name only. - Run test and lint before declaring work done. (Harbor Lane is a made-up example project.) Good entries are surprises: a generated file, an unusual tool, a rule about public copy. Bad entries restate defaults ("write clean code") or hold things that change ("we are working on the webhook"). If a line only repeats what the agent would do anyway, delete it. A rule of thumb is to stay around 40 lines. DECISIONS.md : decision, why, alternatives, revisit-if Every real decision gets a dated entry in a fixed format: ### D-004: Map payments to roles through a config table - Date: 2026-03-11 - Decision: Price identifiers map to tier roles in config/prices.js. - Why: Prices will change; the logic should not. - Alternatives considered: hard-coded if/else on amount (breaks when prices change); a database table (more machinery than three tiers justify). - Revisit if: tiers exceed six, or non-developers need to edit them. - Status: Active Each field does a job: Why lets a future session judge edge cases instead of guessing. Alternatives considered stops the same options being proposed again. Revisit if names the evidence that would justify reopening the choice. Never delete an entry. When you reverse a decision, add a new one that supersedes it and mark the old one Superseded by D-NNN . The history is the point. PROGRESS.md : written for a session that remembers nothing This file answers three questions: where are we, what is blocked, what is next. ## Status board | Phase | State | Gate | |---|---|---| | 1. Website | In progress | npm test passes; pricing page renders | | 2. Payment-to-access | Waiting on Phase 1 | Test-mode payment creates a role and channel | ## Next action Wire the Standard tier payment link into the pricing card; run the render check. ## Blocked - Live payment links: waiting on account verification. Three habits keep it useful: The next action is one concrete step, not a theme. A phase is done only when its gate passes , not when the work feels finished. Update the file at the end of every session, before stopping . A gate for risky work: plan, approve, build For anything that touches money, customer data, going public, or deletion, split the work into three steps: Plan. The agent writes what it will do, in what order, what it will touch, and what could go wrong. It builds nothing. Approve. You read the plan and reply in writing with what you approve and what you change. Build. The agent builds against the approved plan and reports any deviation. Today: the payment webhook handler. Plan first. List the files you will touch, the events you will handle, and the failure cases. Wait for my approval. One detail matters here: an approval you gave in conversation does not exist for the next session. Record it in PROGRESS.md ("Phase 2 webhook plan: approved 2026-03-12 with one change, 7-day activation expiry"). If it is not written down, treat it as not given. And approving a plan is not approving going live. The open-and-close routine Open: paste the master prompt, then add the session line (scope, "read PROGRESS.md first", and the gate if there is one). Close: have the agent update PROGRESS.md (status, next action, blockers). Any new decision gets a DECISIONS.md entry. Ask it to state what it changed and what it did not verify. Reading is reliable; remembering is not. Five minutes of closing routine saves the time you would otherwise spend reconstructing context next time. Try it in 15 minutes Create CLAUDE.md with your commands and only the conventions that surprise a newcomer. Create DECISIONS.md and write down the last three decisions you would hate to re-argue, with the reason for each. Create PROGRESS.md with a status board, one next action, and a blocked list. Next session, start with: "Read PROGRESS.md and DECISIONS.md first, then do X." If a decision keeps coming back, the entry is missing its "why" or its "revisit if". What does your agent keep reopening?
